step1_summary: Chief complaint: Acute shortness of breath with pleuritic right-sided back pain and hemoptysis

Symptoms: Began today with sharp pain in right back on deep inspiration, dyspnea, subjective fever; coughed up small amounts of blood on two occasions; awareness of heartbeat (but measured pulse normal). Reports 2-week history of increased fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.
Past medical history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Medications/allergies: Methotrexate (took a dose this morning); no known drug or other allergies
Family/social history: Non-smoker; works a desk job; lives alone in a flat; has a cat; no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism; no recent long-haul flights

Vital signs/exam (remote): Patient appears stable; radial pulse ~66–74 bpm and regular; normal capillary refill; oropharynx normal; no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy; no objective temperature measured; oxygen saturation and blood pressure not obtained

V: Pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction: Acute pleuritic pain, dyspnea, and minor hemoptysis are classic; SLE increases VTE risk (possible antiphospholipid antibodies), despite no travel or prior VTE.
Pulmonary embolism without infarction: Still possible with dyspnea and pleuritic pain; hemoptysis may be absent or minimal.
I: Community-acquired pneumonia (including pleuritic pneumonia): Fever, pleuritic pain, dyspnea, and hemoptysis; immunosuppression from methotrexate increases risk.
Acute bronchitis: Can cause cough, low-grade fever, dyspnea, and small-volume hemoptysis from airway irritation; pleuritic discomfort may occur.
Tuberculosis: Hemoptysis and constitutional symptoms possible in immunosuppressed host, though abrupt onset today is less typical.
N: Lung cancer: Hemoptysis possible, but acute 1-day presentation with fever and pleuritic pain is atypical; nonsmoker lowers pretest probability.
Bronchial carcinoid: Can cause hemoptysis, but acute febrile pleuritic presentation is less characteristic.
I2: Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis: Dyspnea, cough, fever in patients on methotrexate; hemoptysis less common; onset can be subacute.
Drug-induced cytopenia from methotrexate: Thrombocytopenia could contribute to bleeding (hemoptysis), though no bleeding elsewhere is reported.
C: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (rare/congenital): Could present with hemoptysis and dyspnea; no prior history noted.
A: SLE pleuritis (± small pleural effusion): Causes pleuritic pain and dyspnea; fever can occur in flares; hemoptysis is not typical.
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage due to SLE/vasculitis: Can cause hemoptysis and dyspnea, but usually severe and associated with hypoxia/instability.
T: Spontaneous pneumothorax: Sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnea; hemoptysis is uncommon but possible.
Musculoskeletal chest wall strain: Pleuritic-like pain with deep breath; does not explain hemoptysis.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute onset fever, pleuritic right-sided pain, dyspnea, and minor hemoptysis in an immunosuppressed patient on methotrexate support infectious pneumonia with pleural involvement over other etiologies.

Triad of pleuritic pain, dyspnea, and hemoptysis is characteristic; SLE increases thrombotic risk despite absence of classic provoking factors. Normal heart rate and concurrent fever make PE less likely but do not exclude it.
Cough starting today with low-grade fever and small-volume hemoptysis can be due to acute bronchitis, though pleuritic localized pain and immunosuppression raise concern for pneumonia.
SLE can cause pleuritic chest/back pain and dyspnea with low-grade fever during a flare; hemoptysis is not typical, so this is less likely than infection or PE.
Methotrexate can cause febrile dyspnea and cough, but hemoptysis and abrupt 1-day onset are less typical; pleuritic pain is not classic.

supporting_evidence: Acute pleuritic right-sided back pain on deep inspiration
opposing_evidence: Normal heart rate (66–74 bpm) and appears not acutely unstable
Cough only began today and sputum description limited
No objective temperature or focal lung exam yet

supporting_evidence: Underlying SLE (increased VTE risk, possible antiphospholipid antibodies)
opposing_evidence: No recent long-haul travel, immobilization, prior VTE, or family VTE history
No reported unilateral leg swelling or pain

supporting_evidence: Minor hemoptysis can occur due to airway irritation
opposing_evidence: Localized pleuritic back pain more suggestive of pneumonia or PE
Immunosuppression raises concern for lower respiratory tract infection (pneumonia) rather than simple bronchitis

supporting_evidence: Low-grade fever can occur in flares
opposing_evidence: Hemoptysis not typical for simple pleuritis
No other flare features reported (e.g., rash, arthritis, serositis elsewhere)
Acute cough with blood favors pulmonary pathology
Patient appears stable with normal pulse
